## Paenitentiam Agere: On the Need for the Practice of Interior and Exterior Penance
### About the author
**Pope Saint John XXIII** (Latin: Ioannes XXIII), born **Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli** reigned from 28 October 1958 to his death in 1963.  
He was ordained a priest on 10 August 1904 and served in a number of posts, including papal nuncio in France and a delegate to Bulgaria, Greece, Turkey and Palestine. In a consistory on 12 January 1953 Pope Pius XII made Roncalli a cardinal as the Cardinal-Priest of Santa Prisca in addition to naming him the Patriarch of Venice.
Roncalli was elected pope on 28 October 1958 at age 77 after 11 ballots. His selection was unexpected, and Roncalli himself had come to Rome with a return train ticket to Venice. He was the first pope to take the pontifical name of "John" upon election in more than 500 years, and his choice settled the complicated question of official numbering attached to this papal name due to the antipope of this name.
Pope John XXIII surprised those who expected him to be a caretaker pope by calling the historic Second Vatican Council (1962–65), the first session opening on 11 October 1962. He did not live to see it to completion. John died of stomach cancer on 3 June 1963, four and a half years after his election and two months after the completion of his final and famed encyclical, Pacem in Terris."
He was beatified on 3 September 2000 by Pope John Paul and declared a saint by Pope Francis on 5 July 2013, based on his merits of opening the Second Vatican Council. He was canonised on 27 April 2014. His feast day is 11 October, the day of the first session of the Second Vatican Council.

Title: Offer It Up: Revisiting Penance 60 Years Later
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
T his upcoming Advent marks sixty years since one of the most momentous changes in the history of American Catholicism. One that “may have been the most unnecessary and the most devastating” among the implementations of Vatican II, according to renowned Catholic sociologistAndrew Greely. The impact of this alteration was so far-reaching that most Catholics born after Vatican II are completely unaware that such a dramatic change even occurred for American Catholics.[[1]](https://churchlifejournal.nd.edu/articles/offer-it-up-revisiting-penance-60-years-later/#_ftn1)
In the week prior to November 27, 1966, eating meat on Friday was generally perceived as a mortal sin. Abruptly, however, this was no longer identified as any kind of sin, much less a mortal sin. Year-round Friday meat abstinence had been a significant marker for Catholics in the religiously-pluralistic United States, as was fasting throughout the Lenten season and a number of other social penitential practices, such as fasting prior to big feasts such as Christmas or on Ember Days.
The National Council of Catholic Bishops, predecessor to the USCCB, implemented these dramatic changes in fewer than 2000 words with their “Pastoral Statement on Penance and Abstinence.” The statement was based upon Pope Paul VI’s apostolic constitution_Paenitemini_, which called for the renewal of penance in the worldwide Church and placed the authority to determine the details of penance in the hands of local episcopal conferences.
We will first take a historical overview of Catholic penitential practices in the United States, followed by the demographic context of the changes implemented in 1966.[[2]](https://churchlifejournal.nd.edu/articles/offer-it-up-revisiting-penance-60-years-later/#_ftn2) While aiming to avoid a declension narrative, what follows will nonetheless consider what has been lost as a result of these changes, especially in regard to Catholic identity, community, and discipline.

These are brought into focus by contemporary non-Catholic trends of meatless Mondays, intermittent fasting, and dynorphin-inducing practices like cold-plunges. I conclude by noting that sixty years later the call to renewal of penance still stands. American Catholics today may be among the least penitential of any currently practicing Catholics worldwide, as well as among the least penitential of any Catholics throughout the history of the Church. But do we want it to be this way?

## Historical Notes
Catholics in the United States brought with them the penitential customs from their European origins based on the Church’s canon law for the Latin Rite (i.e. Roman Catholics). These penitential practices were quite strict by today’s standards. They included “one meal a day, abstinence from meat, abstinence from eggs and milk products during Lent, and abstinence from fish at those meals where meat was eaten on a fast day as well as on Sundays of Lent. Abstinence from meat without fasting was observed by general law on all Fridays and Saturdays throughout the year,” as described in greater detail in my book_Sin in the Sixties_ Chapters 1 and 4 _._
The limited nutritional circumstances of Catholics in the United States resulted in the Vatican making numerous exceptions to penance, such as allowing for American Catholics to eat meat on five of the six Sundays of Lent. In 1837, the pope dropped fasting for Wednesdays and Fridays of Advent and abstaining from meat on Wednesdays of Advent, and in 1886 Leo XII dispensed from meat abstinence on Saturdays for all American dioceses. Leo XIII permitted American Catholics to use meat, eggs, and milk products at all meals on Sundays during Lent and at the principal (i.e. main or full) meal Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday. Additionally, in 1895 the so-called “workingman’s privilege” allowed American Catholics to eat meat once a day when there was difficulty in observing common law. This indult originally only applied to a manual laborer and his family, but in 1951 it was extended to all American Catholics in a move for uniformity of practice.
Thus, we can see that even prior to Vatican II and Paul VI’s _Paenitemini_, American Catholics already had been granted many reductions to the Church’s expected penitential practices. However, the remaining practices of year-round Friday meat abstinence, Lenten fasting, Ember Days fasting, etc. remained firmly entrenched in American Catholic subculture. At the close of Vatican II, Paul VI was eager for a renewal of penance and looked to the local bishops’ conferences to take the lead, based on what they could determine was best for their region.

## _Paenitentiam Agere_, Vatican II, and _Paenitemini:_ Revisiting Penance 60 Years Later
Prior to the Second Vatican Council, John XXIII released his encyclical _Paenitentiam Agere_ (July 1962), beginning with these words:
> Doing penance for one's sins is a first step towards obtaining forgiveness and winning eternal salvation. That is the clear and explicit teaching of Christ, and no one can fail to see how justified and how right the Catholic Church has always been in constantly insisting on this. She is the spokesman for her divine Redeemer. No individual Christian can grow in perfection, nor can Christianity gain in vigor, except it be on the basis of penance.
Pope John then emphasized the importance of penance in preparation for the council: interior and exterior, individual and social, private and public. While penance was prescribed by the Church at certain times, John also noted “the acceptance from God in a spirit of resignation and trust of all life's sorrows and hardships and of everything that involves inconvenience and annoyance in the conscientious performance of the obligations of our daily life and work and the practice of Christian virtue” (§30). Colloquially, this was associated with the phrase, “Offer it up!”
John XXIII’s _Paenitentiam Agere_ and Paul VI’s _Paenitemini_ thus serve as bookends of Vatican II. While the first was precursory for council work, the second was a fruit and implementation of the council. Paul VI was eager to remind the faithful of the grave and urgent problem “of the significance and importance of the divine precept of penitence.” Like John, Paul recognized that the Church was “in continuous need of conversion and renewal, a renewal which must be implemented not only interiorly and individually but also externally and socially.”
In no way did Paul VI intend for the Church to move beyond penance; Vatican II did not herald a post-penitential Church. The pope rather viewed penance as essential for realizing the fruits of the council. Paul indicated that renewal might involve seeking out penitential practices beyond fast and abstinence (Ch. 2). Though he listed the universal prescriptive penances for Catholics globally, Paul also gave local episcopal conferences the authority to substitute other practices for fast and abstinence, indicating his eagerness for the renewal of penance in a modern setting.

## _Paenitentiam Agere_, Vatican II, and _Paenitemini:_ Revisiting Penance 60 Years Later
The American NCCB’s “Pastoral Statement on Penance and Abstinence” took the call for renewal of penance in _Paenitemini_ and enacted the practical changes in the U.S. While the content of this statement is crucial to understanding the details, the American context—both sociologically and theologically—frames the reception of these changes.
As noted above, Friday meat abstinence had been a Catholic identity marker for years in a religiously pluralistic country. American Catholics often made their home in urban ethnic conclaves, with separate parishes for Italians, Irish, Germans, Polish, etc. Catholics maintained their identity and religious practices in such a homogenous social setting. During and after World War II, American identity increased for Catholics. The initially poor immigrant Catholics relegated to manual labor were now established, and their children and grandchildren experienced upward social and economic mobility. Younger generations were now able to leave the urban Catholic subculture for American suburban life, and consequently traditional Catholic practices were not a natural part of their world but were rather experienced as external impositions by authority.
As they emerged from Catholic subculture, clerics and laity alike articulated criticisms of Catholic practice. One particularly negative assessment noted the “unthinking obedience” of Catholic required routines: eating fish on Fridays, lining up for confession on Saturdays, mumbling prayers in Latin on Sunday, and basically doing whatever they were told they had to do. Such obedience came under fire; adherence to Church practice seemed to be a mark of immaturity rather than humility.
Germany in World War II had demonstrated the danger of obedience to authority, and now many Americans objected to the conflict in Vietnam, as well as calling attention to longstanding racial injustices in the United States. Authority, obligation, obedience were all imbued with a negative connotation; autonomy, freedom, and choice now took precedence. For some, the spirit of Vatican II appeared in accord with this trend. Unlike previous councils, there were no anathemas proclaimed in condemning errors; Vatican II seemed to embrace the world, rather than object to it.

T his upcoming Advent marks sixty years since one of the most momentous changes in the history of American Catholicism. One that “may have been the most unnecessary and the most devastating” among the implementations of Vatican II, according to renowned Catholic sociologistAndrew Greely. The impact of this alteration was so far-reaching that most Catholics born after Vatican II are completely unaware that such a dramatic change even occurred for American Catholics.[[1]](https://churchlifejournal.nd.edu/articles/offer-it-up-revisiting-penance-60-years-later/#_ftn1)
In the week prior to November 27, 1966, eating meat on Friday was generally perceived as a mortal sin. Abruptly, however, this was no longer identified as any kind of sin, much less a mortal sin. Year-round Friday meat abstinence had been a significant marker for Catholics in the religiously-pluralistic United States, as was fasting throughout the Lenten season and a number of other social penitential practices, such as fasting prior to big feasts such as Christmas or on Ember Days.
The National Council of Catholic Bishops, predecessor to the USCCB, implemented these dramatic changes in fewer than 2000 words with their “Pastoral Statement on Penance and Abstinence.” The statement was based upon Pope Paul VI’s apostolic constitution_Paenitemini_, which called for the renewal of penance in the worldwide Church and placed the authority to determine the details of penance in the hands of local episcopal conferences.
We will first take a historical overview of Catholic penitential practices in the United States, followed by the demographic context of the changes implemented in 1966.[[2]](https://churchlifejournal.nd.edu/articles/offer-it-up-revisiting-penance-60-years-later/#_ftn2) While aiming to avoid a declension narrative, what follows will nonetheless consider what has been lost as a result of these changes, especially in regard to Catholic identity, community, and discipline.
texts.1: These are brought into focus by contemporary non-Catholic trends of meatless Mondays, intermittent fasting, and dynorphin-inducing practices like cold-plunges. I conclude by noting that sixty years later the call to renewal of penance still stands. American Catholics today may be among the least penitential of any currently practicing Catholics worldwide, as well as among the least penitential of any Catholics throughout the history of the Church. But do we want it to be this way?

## Historical Notes
Catholics in the United States brought with them the penitential customs from their European origins based on the Church’s canon law for the Latin Rite (i.e. Roman Catholics). These penitential practices were quite strict by today’s standards. They included “one meal a day, abstinence from meat, abstinence from eggs and milk products during Lent, and abstinence from fish at those meals where meat was eaten on a fast day as well as on Sundays of Lent. Abstinence from meat without fasting was observed by general law on all Fridays and Saturdays throughout the year,” as described in greater detail in my book_Sin in the Sixties_ Chapters 1 and 4 _._
The limited nutritional circumstances of Catholics in the United States resulted in the Vatican making numerous exceptions to penance, such as allowing for American Catholics to eat meat on five of the six Sundays of Lent. In 1837, the pope dropped fasting for Wednesdays and Fridays of Advent and abstaining from meat on Wednesdays of Advent, and in 1886 Leo XII dispensed from meat abstinence on Saturdays for all American dioceses. Leo XIII permitted American Catholics to use meat, eggs, and milk products at all meals on Sundays during Lent and at the principal (i.e. main or full) meal Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday. Additionally, in 1895 the so-called “workingman’s privilege” allowed American Catholics to eat meat once a day when there was difficulty in observing common law. This indult originally only applied to a manual laborer and his family, but in 1951 it was extended to all American Catholics in a move for uniformity of practice.
Thus, we can see that even prior to Vatican II and Paul VI’s _Paenitemini_, American Catholics already had been granted many reductions to the Church’s expected penitential practices. However, the remaining practices of year-round Friday meat abstinence, Lenten fasting, Ember Days fasting, etc. remained firmly entrenched in American Catholic subculture. At the close of Vatican II, Paul VI was eager for a renewal of penance and looked to the local bishops’ conferences to take the lead, based on what they could determine was best for their region.

## _Paenitentiam Agere_, Vatican II, and _Paenitemini:_ Revisiting Penance 60 Years Later
Prior to the Second Vatican Council, John XXIII released his encyclical _Paenitentiam Agere_ (July 1962), beginning with these words:
> Doing penance for one's sins is a first step towards obtaining forgiveness and winning eternal salvation. That is the clear and explicit teaching of Christ, and no one can fail to see how justified and how right the Catholic Church has always been in constantly insisting on this. She is the spokesman for her divine Redeemer. No individual Christian can grow in perfection, nor can Christianity gain in vigor, except it be on the basis of penance.
Pope John then emphasized the importance of penance in preparation for the council: interior and exterior, individual and social, private and public. While penance was prescribed by the Church at certain times, John also noted “the acceptance from God in a spirit of resignation and trust of all life's sorrows and hardships and of everything that involves inconvenience and annoyance in the conscientious performance of the obligations of our daily life and work and the practice of Christian virtue” (§30). Colloquially, this was associated with the phrase, “Offer it up!”
John XXIII’s _Paenitentiam Agere_ and Paul VI’s _Paenitemini_ thus serve as bookends of Vatican II. While the first was precursory for council work, the second was a fruit and implementation of the council. Paul VI was eager to remind the faithful of the grave and urgent problem “of the significance and importance of the divine precept of penitence.” Like John, Paul recognized that the Church was “in continuous need of conversion and renewal, a renewal which must be implemented not only interiorly and individually but also externally and socially.”
In no way did Paul VI intend for the Church to move beyond penance; Vatican II did not herald a post-penitential Church. The pope rather viewed penance as essential for realizing the fruits of the council. Paul indicated that renewal might involve seeking out penitential practices beyond fast and abstinence (Ch. 2). Though he listed the universal prescriptive penances for Catholics globally, Paul also gave local episcopal conferences the authority to substitute other practices for fast and abstinence, indicating his eagerness for the renewal of penance in a modern setting.
texts.4:
## _Paenitentiam Agere_, Vatican II, and _Paenitemini:_ Revisiting Penance 60 Years Later
The American NCCB’s “Pastoral Statement on Penance and Abstinence” took the call for renewal of penance in _Paenitemini_ and enacted the practical changes in the U.S. While the content of this statement is crucial to understanding the details, the American context—both sociologically and theologically—frames the reception of these changes.
As noted above, Friday meat abstinence had been a Catholic identity marker for years in a religiously pluralistic country. American Catholics often made their home in urban ethnic conclaves, with separate parishes for Italians, Irish, Germans, Polish, etc. Catholics maintained their identity and religious practices in such a homogenous social setting. During and after World War II, American identity increased for Catholics. The initially poor immigrant Catholics relegated to manual labor were now established, and their children and grandchildren experienced upward social and economic mobility. Younger generations were now able to leave the urban Catholic subculture for American suburban life, and consequently traditional Catholic practices were not a natural part of their world but were rather experienced as external impositions by authority.
As they emerged from Catholic subculture, clerics and laity alike articulated criticisms of Catholic practice. One particularly negative assessment noted the “unthinking obedience” of Catholic required routines: eating fish on Fridays, lining up for confession on Saturdays, mumbling prayers in Latin on Sunday, and basically doing whatever they were told they had to do. Such obedience came under fire; adherence to Church practice seemed to be a mark of immaturity rather than humility.
Germany in World War II had demonstrated the danger of obedience to authority, and now many Americans objected to the conflict in Vietnam, as well as calling attention to longstanding racial injustices in the United States. Authority, obligation, obedience were all imbued with a negative connotation; autonomy, freedom, and choice now took precedence. For some, the spirit of Vatican II appeared in accord with this trend. Unlike previous councils, there were no anathemas proclaimed in condemning errors; Vatican II seemed to embrace the world, rather than object to it.

### About the author
**Pope Saint John XXIII** (Latin: Ioannes XXIII), born **Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli** reigned from 28 October 1958 to his death in 1963.  
He was ordained a priest on 10 August 1904 and served in a number of posts, including papal nuncio in France and a delegate to Bulgaria, Greece, Turkey and Palestine. In a consistory on 12 January 1953 Pope Pius XII made Roncalli a cardinal as the Cardinal-Priest of Santa Prisca in addition to naming him the Patriarch of Venice.
Roncalli was elected pope on 28 October 1958 at age 77 after 11 ballots. His selection was unexpected, and Roncalli himself had come to Rome with a return train ticket to Venice. He was the first pope to take the pontifical name of "John" upon election in more than 500 years, and his choice settled the complicated question of official numbering attached to this papal name due to the antipope of this name.
Pope John XXIII surprised those who expected him to be a caretaker pope by calling the historic Second Vatican Council (1962–65), the first session opening on 11 October 1962. He did not live to see it to completion. John died of stomach cancer on 3 June 1963, four and a half years after his election and two months after the completion of his final and famed encyclical, Pacem in Terris."
He was beatified on 3 September 2000 by Pope John Paul and declared a saint by Pope Francis on 5 July 2013, based on his merits of opening the Second Vatican Council. He was canonised on 27 April 2014. His feast day is 11 October, the day of the first session of the Second Vatican Council.

Title: Offer It Up: Revisiting Penance 60 Years Later
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
T his upcoming Advent marks sixty years since one of the most momentous changes in the history of American Catholicism. One that “may have been the most unnecessary and the most devastating” among the implementations of Vatican II, according to renowned Catholic sociologistAndrew Greely. The impact of this alteration was so far-reaching that most Catholics born after Vatican II are completely unaware that such a dramatic change even occurred for American Catholics.[[1]](https://churchlifejournal.nd.edu/articles/offer-it-up-revisiting-penance-60-years-later/#_ftn1)
In the week prior to November 27, 1966, eating meat on Friday was generally perceived as a mortal sin. Abruptly, however, this was no longer identified as any kind of sin, much less a mortal sin. Year-round Friday meat abstinence had been a significant marker for Catholics in the religiously-pluralistic United States, as was fasting throughout the Lenten season and a number of other social penitential practices, such as fasting prior to big feasts such as Christmas or on Ember Days.
The National Council of Catholic Bishops, predecessor to the USCCB, implemented these dramatic changes in fewer than 2000 words with their “Pastoral Statement on Penance and Abstinence.” The statement was based upon Pope Paul VI’s apostolic constitution_Paenitemini_, which called for the renewal of penance in the worldwide Church and placed the authority to determine the details of penance in the hands of local episcopal conferences.
We will first take a historical overview of Catholic penitential practices in the United States, followed by the demographic context of the changes implemented in 1966.[[2]](https://churchlifejournal.nd.edu/articles/offer-it-up-revisiting-penance-60-years-later/#_ftn2) While aiming to avoid a declension narrative, what follows will nonetheless consider what has been lost as a result of these changes, especially in regard to Catholic identity, community, and discipline.

These are brought into focus by contemporary non-Catholic trends of meatless Mondays, intermittent fasting, and dynorphin-inducing practices like cold-plunges. I conclude by noting that sixty years later the call to renewal of penance still stands. American Catholics today may be among the least penitential of any currently practicing Catholics worldwide, as well as among the least penitential of any Catholics throughout the history of the Church. But do we want it to be this way?

## Historical Notes
Catholics in the United States brought with them the penitential customs from their European origins based on the Church’s canon law for the Latin Rite (i.e. Roman Catholics). These penitential practices were quite strict by today’s standards. They included “one meal a day, abstinence from meat, abstinence from eggs and milk products during Lent, and abstinence from fish at those meals where meat was eaten on a fast day as well as on Sundays of Lent. Abstinence from meat without fasting was observed by general law on all Fridays and Saturdays throughout the year,” as described in greater detail in my book_Sin in the Sixties_ Chapters 1 and 4 _._
The limited nutritional circumstances of Catholics in the United States resulted in the Vatican making numerous exceptions to penance, such as allowing for American Catholics to eat meat on five of the six Sundays of Lent. In 1837, the pope dropped fasting for Wednesdays and Fridays of Advent and abstaining from meat on Wednesdays of Advent, and in 1886 Leo XII dispensed from meat abstinence on Saturdays for all American dioceses. Leo XIII permitted American Catholics to use meat, eggs, and milk products at all meals on Sundays during Lent and at the principal (i.e. main or full) meal Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday. Additionally, in 1895 the so-called “workingman’s privilege” allowed American Catholics to eat meat once a day when there was difficulty in observing common law. This indult originally only applied to a manual laborer and his family, but in 1951 it was extended to all American Catholics in a move for uniformity of practice.
Thus, we can see that even prior to Vatican II and Paul VI’s _Paenitemini_, American Catholics already had been granted many reductions to the Church’s expected penitential practices. However, the remaining practices of year-round Friday meat abstinence, Lenten fasting, Ember Days fasting, etc. remained firmly entrenched in American Catholic subculture. At the close of Vatican II, Paul VI was eager for a renewal of penance and looked to the local bishops’ conferences to take the lead, based on what they could determine was best for their region.

## _Paenitentiam Agere_, Vatican II, and _Paenitemini:_ Revisiting Penance 60 Years Later
Prior to the Second Vatican Council, John XXIII released his encyclical _Paenitentiam Agere_ (July 1962), beginning with these words:
> Doing penance for one's sins is a first step towards obtaining forgiveness and winning eternal salvation. That is the clear and explicit teaching of Christ, and no one can fail to see how justified and how right the Catholic Church has always been in constantly insisting on this. She is the spokesman for her divine Redeemer. No individual Christian can grow in perfection, nor can Christianity gain in vigor, except it be on the basis of penance.
Pope John then emphasized the importance of penance in preparation for the council: interior and exterior, individual and social, private and public. While penance was prescribed by the Church at certain times, John also noted “the acceptance from God in a spirit of resignation and trust of all life's sorrows and hardships and of everything that involves inconvenience and annoyance in the conscientious performance of the obligations of our daily life and work and the practice of Christian virtue” (§30). Colloquially, this was associated with the phrase, “Offer it up!”
John XXIII’s _Paenitentiam Agere_ and Paul VI’s _Paenitemini_ thus serve as bookends of Vatican II. While the first was precursory for council work, the second was a fruit and implementation of the council. Paul VI was eager to remind the faithful of the grave and urgent problem “of the significance and importance of the divine precept of penitence.” Like John, Paul recognized that the Church was “in continuous need of conversion and renewal, a renewal which must be implemented not only interiorly and individually but also externally and socially.”
In no way did Paul VI intend for the Church to move beyond penance; Vatican II did not herald a post-penitential Church. The pope rather viewed penance as essential for realizing the fruits of the council. Paul indicated that renewal might involve seeking out penitential practices beyond fast and abstinence (Ch. 2). Though he listed the universal prescriptive penances for Catholics globally, Paul also gave local episcopal conferences the authority to substitute other practices for fast and abstinence, indicating his eagerness for the renewal of penance in a modern setting.

## _Paenitentiam Agere_, Vatican II, and _Paenitemini:_ Revisiting Penance 60 Years Later
The American NCCB’s “Pastoral Statement on Penance and Abstinence” took the call for renewal of penance in _Paenitemini_ and enacted the practical changes in the U.S. While the content of this statement is crucial to understanding the details, the American context—both sociologically and theologically—frames the reception of these changes.
As noted above, Friday meat abstinence had been a Catholic identity marker for years in a religiously pluralistic country. American Catholics often made their home in urban ethnic conclaves, with separate parishes for Italians, Irish, Germans, Polish, etc. Catholics maintained their identity and religious practices in such a homogenous social setting. During and after World War II, American identity increased for Catholics. The initially poor immigrant Catholics relegated to manual labor were now established, and their children and grandchildren experienced upward social and economic mobility. Younger generations were now able to leave the urban Catholic subculture for American suburban life, and consequently traditional Catholic practices were not a natural part of their world but were rather experienced as external impositions by authority.
As they emerged from Catholic subculture, clerics and laity alike articulated criticisms of Catholic practice. One particularly negative assessment noted the “unthinking obedience” of Catholic required routines: eating fish on Fridays, lining up for confession on Saturdays, mumbling prayers in Latin on Sunday, and basically doing whatever they were told they had to do. Such obedience came under fire; adherence to Church practice seemed to be a mark of immaturity rather than humility.
Germany in World War II had demonstrated the danger of obedience to authority, and now many Americans objected to the conflict in Vietnam, as well as calling attention to longstanding racial injustices in the United States. Authority, obligation, obedience were all imbued with a negative connotation; autonomy, freedom, and choice now took precedence. For some, the spirit of Vatican II appeared in accord with this trend. Unlike previous councils, there were no anathemas proclaimed in condemning errors; Vatican II seemed to embrace the world, rather than object to it.
